title: The Ode in Quatrains, on Admonition and the Sunna
intro: Jamal al-Din Abd al-Qahir al-Tabrizi, a Shafi'i judge and preacher who grew up in Damascus, recited this poem to his student al-Dhahabi in 704 AH (1304 CE); al-Dhahabi copied it in full into his dictionary of his teachers and elsewhere called it “an admonition that reminds”. It opens like a love poem, with the ban trees, Rama and La'la' of the old Arabian lovers, then shows that the longing is for a higher home, and turns to prayer at night and tears, to the Sunni creed on the Quran and on God's attributes, to the Scales, Hell and Paradise, and ends in prayer and a blessing on the Prophet. Each of its 22 stanzas has four short lines in the rajaz metre: the first three share a rhyme that changes from stanza to stanza, and the fourth always ends on the letter ayn, a form that suits the name it goes by today, al-Ruba'iyya, “the poem in fours”. Al-Dhahabi reports that the judge al-Qazwini dismissed him and condemned his creed “because he did not explain away but affirmed”, the position the middle stanzas set out.

translation: How many, among the ban trees of al-Ajra', at Rama and La'la',
are the aching hearts of lovers, drunk with longing and senseless.
1.sharh: Countless lovers' hearts lie among the trees and campsites of the old love poems, too drunk with longing to know anything. He opens as the old poets did, with places Arabic love poetry made famous.

translation: You see him among fine robes, wounded by the swords of eyes;
be gentle with him, and do not ask about his lost heart.
2.sharh: The lover wears rich robes, a man of standing, yet glances sharp as swords have cut him down. Be gentle with him, and do not ask where his heart has gone: it is lost.

translation: He loved the sanctuary truly, since its claim had become plain,
and his wish is to be set free from the lowest depths,
3.sharh: He gave the sanctuary his whole love, and wants only to rise out of the depths: the love is for something higher than a woman. Akhlasa (he loved truly) and yakhlusa (be set free) share a root.

translation: and reach his first home, the sweet place where he knew companionship,
that high and lofty dwelling: may rain fall on it, what a home.
4.sharh: He longs for his first home and prays for rain on it. Al-Zahrani takes it as Bukhara, where his family came from, or Harran, where he was born; it may also be Paradise, mankind's first home.

translation: I left that open land, not by my choice or my will;
time that has passed, if what is past ever returns, come back.
5.sharh: He left that land against his will, and calls on the past to return, knowing it never does. So what remains of life must be spent well, which is where the poem turns next.

translation: Bow down when night grows dark, a bowing of fear and hope,
and cross in the ships of salvation to the widest of spaces.
6.sharh: Pray at night, fearing God and hoping in Him, and let good deeds carry you like ships to Paradise, the widest of spaces. He has lost one open land (line 5) and is shown a wider one.

translation: Keep the night vigil, stand long and bow to the ground;
spend the night as the star's companion, and drink cups of tears.
7.sharh: Pray through the night, standing long and lying long in prostration. He borrows the language of the wine party: sit up with a star for company, and let your cups be tears shed in awe of God.

translation: Stop where the Book has ruled, and do not swerve from it,
and do not plunge, God guide you, into what innovators say.
8.sharh: Hold to what the Quran decides, and do not wade into the doctrines of those who invent new beliefs: whoever goes past the Book follows opinion, and opinion leads to whim.

translation: For it is His speech; its composition has defeated all creation,
and its shining rulings have dazzled every faction.
9.sharh: The Quran is God's own speech: no one has matched the way it is composed, and its clear rulings have overwhelmed every sect. Two doctrines meet here: the Quran cannot be imitated, and it is truly God's speech.

translation: From Him it came forth, as it has reached us; lean on it,
and argue with no one over its verses; hold back.
10.sharh: The Quran came from God and has reached us unchanged; rely on it, and never dispute anyone over its verses. The line echoes the early creed: “From Him it came, and to Him it returns”.

translation: Do not explain away what scripture ascribes to God, hearing and hand,
and say “He is God, One” as a man who follows.
11.sharh: Do not turn what scripture says of God, His hearing or His hand, into metaphor; affirm it as it came, and declare His oneness as one who follows the Prophet's way, not one who invents.

translation: And He, mighty and majestic, spoke to Moses, who was afraid,
when He showed Himself to the mountain, aloud, in speech that was heard.
12.sharh: God truly speaks: He spoke to Moses, who stood in fear, when He appeared to the mountain, aloud, in words Moses heard. The Quran says it plainly: “God spoke to Moses directly”.

translation: Moses listened, and took in with his ear what he heard,
then answered at once, the answer of a steadfast, noble man.
13.sharh: Moses heard God's words with his own ears and took them in, then answered without hesitating, firm of heart. The point is doctrinal: God's speech was real sound, heard by a human ear.

translation: Do not side with one who strays; say that the Lord of strength
truly rose over the Throne, as He willed. So hear.
14.sharh: Do not agree with those who have gone astray: God truly rose over His Throne, in the way He willed. The Quran says so in seven places; the early scholars held that its meaning is known and its manner is not.

translation: Exalted, He is high in the heaven, and with us wherever we are,
without our asking how, and not as the innovator imagines.
15.sharh: God is high above His creation and yet with us wherever we are, as the Quran says. It is not what the innovator imagines; Sunni creed reads this nearness as His knowledge and care.

translation: Whoever among men measures Him against His creatures has disbelieved,
and has obeyed and championed the command of the whim he follows.
16.sharh: Anyone who likens God to the things He made has left the faith, obeying his own whims and fighting for them. To affirm God's attributes is not to make Him like anything, for nothing is like Him.

translation: Woe at the weighing of deeds: with me, their sea is a trickle;
its swelling waters have sunk and dwindled; the spring shows nothing.
17.sharh: He dreads the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgement: what should be a sea of good works is, with him, a trickle that has dried up. After advising others, he turns on himself.

translation: Hell is set in the way, its fire blazing,
the sinner thrown in face first, and it is said: “Fire, swallow.”
18.sharh: Hell is brought forward, blazing; the sinner is flung in, and the fire is told to swallow. The past tense makes the future certain, and “Fire, swallow” echoes the Quran's “Earth, swallow your water” at the end of the Flood.

translation: Paradise, Firdaws, has put on its finery for the man who worshipped,
stood at night and bowed to the ground in his patched old rag.
19.sharh: Paradise has dressed itself up for the one who prayed by night in a patched old garment. The finery waits there for those who went without it here; the rag answers the rich robes of line 2.

translation: Its maidens' breasts have rounded, its rivers run on and on,
its birds sing on every branch heavy with ripe fruit.
20.sharh: The delights of Paradise: maidens in their first bloom, rivers that never stop, birds singing on every ripening branch, all drawn from the Quran's pictures of the Garden.

translation: You to whom I give myself in every pitch-dark night,
to whom I turn for refuge, and no one else, my shelter,
21.sharh: He ends in prayer to God, to whom he gives himself in the darkest nights, his one refuge besides whom there is none. The nights recall the vigil he urged in line 7.

translation: bless the best of mankind, of every woman and man,
Muhammad, the moon's face, whose side is guarded.
22.sharh: He closes by asking God to bless Muhammad, the best of all people, whose face shines like the moon. Scholars customarily ended a poem or a teaching verse this way.

1.1.3.head: بان
1.1.3.meaning: Ban: a tall tree with long, supple branches, to which poets liken a graceful figure.

1.1.4.head: الأَجرَع
1.1.4.meaning: Ajra': a stretch of ground mixed with sand; al-Zahrani takes it as a place in al-Yamama.

1.1.5.head: رامَة
1.1.5.meaning: Rama: a halt on the road from Basra to Mecca, according to Yaqut, and a name that recurs in Arabic love poetry.

1.1.6.head: لَعلَع
1.1.6.meaning: La'la': a place on the pilgrim road from Basra.

1.2.3.head: صَبّ
1.2.3.meaning: Sabb: a lover burning with longing.

2.1.4.meaning: Hulal: fine robes; a hulla is a matching wrap and mantle.

3.1.2.meaning: Hima: a tract of land closed to outsiders; in love poetry, the beloved's country.

3.1.7.head: حَصحَصَ
3.1.7.meaning: Has come to light. The Quran uses it of Joseph's innocence: “Now the truth has come to light” (12:51).

3.2.5.head: الحَضيض
3.2.5.meaning: Hadid: the low ground at the foot of a mountain; here, a base and lowly state.

7.1.2.head: التَّهَجُّد
7.1.2.meaning: Tahajjud: voluntary prayer at night, after some sleep.

7.2.2.head: نَديم
7.2.2.meaning: Nadim: a drinking companion, the friend who sits up through the night with you.

7.2.3.head: الفَرقَد
7.2.3.meaning: Farqad: a star near the Pole Star, one of a pair that travellers steered by; the two are a byword for lasting companionship.

8.2.3.head: وُفِّقَ
8.2.3.meaning: “May you be guided”: a prayer set inside the warning. Al-Dhahabi's and al-Zahrani's texts have waqa'ta, “you have fallen”.

8.2.7.head: البِدَع
8.2.7.meaning: Bid'a: a practice or belief brought into religion that the Prophet and his Companions did not hold.

9.2.5.head: الشِّيَع
9.2.5.meaning: Shiya': factions, sects of every kind, not the Shia in particular.

10.1.7.head: مُعتَضِد
10.1.7.meaning: Leaning on it for strength; from adud, the upper arm.

10.2.5.head: آي
10.2.5.meaning: Its verses: ay, plural of aya, a verse of the Quran. Al-Dhahabi's and al-Zahrani's texts have “a verse”.

11.1.2.head: أَوَّلَ
11.1.2.meaning: Ta'wil: reading a text away from its plain sense, for example taking God's “hand” to mean His power.

11.2.1-4.meaning: “Say: He is God, One”: the opening of Surat al-Ikhlas (112), on God's oneness.

12.2.2-3.meaning: “Showed Himself to the mountain”: the Quran tells how, when God appeared to the mountain, it crumbled to dust and Moses fell senseless (7:143).

12.2.6.meaning: Musmi': making itself heard. Grammar calls for musmi'an, agreeing with kalaman; the rhyme turns it to musmi'i.

13.2.6.head: أَروَع
13.2.6.meaning: Arwa': a man whose looks or courage strike you with awe.

14.1.7-8.meaning: “Possessor of strength”: God, whom the Quran calls “Possessor of strength, the Firm” (51:58).

14.2.4.meaning: Rose over: the Quran's word for God's relation to His Throne, “The Merciful rose over the Throne” (20:5).

15.1.6.head: مَع
15.1.6.meaning: “And with us”: ma'na, an old variant of ma'ana. Al-Hayla's edition of al-Dhahabi prints the homophone ma'na, “meaning”.

15.2.1-2.meaning: “Without how”: without asking how; the creed's formula bi-la kayf.

17.1.7.meaning: Washal: a trickle of water oozing from a rock.

19.1.2.head: الفِردَوس
19.1.2.meaning: Firdaws: the highest garden of Paradise, which the Prophet told believers to ask God for.

19.2.5.head: طِمر
19.2.5.meaning: Timr: a worn-out garment. A hadith speaks of the dishevelled man in two rags whom no one notices, yet whose oath God would fulfil.

20.1.2.head: أَبكار
20.1.2.meaning: “Virgins”: the houris of Paradise; the Quran says “We made them virgins” (56:36).

21.1.4.head: تَبَتُّل
21.1.4.meaning: Tabattul: giving oneself wholly to God; the Quran commands “devote yourself to Him completely” (73:8).

22.2.5-6.meaning: “Guarded side”: honour that no one can touch.
